rappel_detail.notes: First of four double-rope rappels down the East Face, starting near M&M Ledge.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor, climber's-left of M&M Ledge
hazards: The M&M Ledge anchor is two pieces of old fixed gear, a pin and a wire. A large and reportedly bomber horn sits up and left of it that would make a much better station and nobody has rigged it - carry cord if you want to use it
Because the line trends left rather than dropping straight down, a rope end blown or thrown off line is awkward to recover
rappel_detail.station: The rappels begin at M&M Ledge. From it, work climber's left to reach good bolts - the bolted stations are not directly beneath where the ledge drops you, and finding them is the only route-finding on this descent. If you rappel from the ledge's own anchor instead, that is a fixed piton and a fixed wire, and the rappel from it also trends climber's left.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the East Face line on double ropes.
hazards: Steep sustained face with nothing to stand on between stations - once on the rope you are committed to reaching the next anchor
rappel_detail.station: Second station on the bolted line down the East Face.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the East Face line on double ropes.
hazards: Anything knocked off a station here falls the full height of the wall
rappel_detail.station: Third station on the bolted line.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel, reaching the ground at the base of the East Face.
hazards: Talus and snow at the base of the face for much of the season
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel, essentially reaching the ground at the base of the East Face - the side you approached from, so this is where your pack is.

wa_liberty_bell_thin_red_line.rappels: 4 double-rope rappels from bolted anchors down the East Face, starting climber’s left of M&M Ledge
wa_liberty_bell_thin_red_line.rappel_count_note: Four rappels off bolts, reached by working climber's left from M&M Ledge, and the description that gives that sequence assumes two ropes - four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground. Parties who first rappel from M&M Ledge's own fixed pin-and-wire anchor, which also trends climber's left, count five. No single-rope option is described for this line. The alternative descent, for parties who continue to the true summit rather than rappelling from the ledge, is the standard Liberty Bell notch route - a downclimb east to a two-bolt station and two rappels of about 25 m into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch - which is fewer rappels but lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face approach and from your pack. Per-station distances are not published; the figures given assume near-full-length double-rope rappels.
wa_liberty_bell_thin_red_line.descent_text: Two documented options. (1) From the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels (2 ropes) essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face — this is the faster option and returns you directly to your pack/the East Face approach. (2) If you continue to the true summit instead, descend via the standard Liberty Bell notch route: downclimb east ~100 ft through trees/loose rock to the 2-bolt station, then make two roughly 25m rappels (the second off a bolted anchor) down into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then hike down the scree/snow gully to the climbers' trail along the base of the west faces — but this leaves you on the opposite (west) side of the mountain from your car at the East Face pullout, requiring a shuttle or road walk back.

rappel_detail.pull: Under 30m, single 60m rope. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch — that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes.
rappel_detail.notes: After topping out, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to a bolted anchor in an alcove; first rappel down toward Beckey Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor (double-bolt station in an alcove near the topout)
hazards: the last few metres to the anchor cross an exposed sloping ledge
the station is genuinely hard to spot from above and parties have rappelled past the line or had to climb back up to find it; note it before you commit to going down
rappel_detail.station: Reached by traversing climber's left along the third-class ledges at the top of the route, or by downclimbing the last pitch of the Beckey Route. The anchor is shiny bolts with chains set in a corner or shallow alcove on a steep wall overlooking the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — you have to look down over the edge a little to see it, and it is not visible from the ledge above.

rappel_detail.pull: About 25m, single 60m rope reaches the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel reaches Beckey Gully / the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch; from there downclimb/hike the gully to the climbers' trail.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor (the second station is also described as a tree — judge what is there)
hazards: this last rappel is the one repeatedly reported for stuck ropes, in more than one case costing a party a re-lead of an adjacent route to recover the strand

you are rappelling over a climbing route and above a busy approach gully, so both your rope and anything you knock loose land on other parties — the notch echoes badly enough that shouted communication is unreliable when it is busy
the notch below is snow early or loose scree later, and the gully leading down from it sheds rock readily
rappel_detail.station: A second set of bolts and chains, described as sitting in an alcove with a tree beside it, dropping directly into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.

wa_liberty_crack.descent_text:
The standard way off is the two-rappel Beckey-side descent, shared with Liberty Crack (Free), Freedom Rider and the Beckey Route. From the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder where the last pitch ends, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to the double-bolt station - the final few metres to it are exposed - and make the first rappel, under 30 m, down toward Beckey Gully. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch: that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes. A second rappel of roughly the same length reaches Beckey Gully and the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch, and from there you downclimb and hike the scree and boulder gully below the notch - snow-covered or loose and unpleasant depending on the season - to the climbers' trail and the Blue Lake Trail. Manage the ropes carefully on both: the terrain is steep and snags are the common problem here.

Plan the walk back before you start down. Liberty Crack parties park at the East Face pullout on SR-20 rather than at the Blue Lake Trailhead, so this descent puts you down on the far side of the mountain from the car, meaning either a shuttle or roughly a mile back along the highway shoulder. A rappel line down the east face that returns you directly to your packs at the base of the route has been reported - a bolted line of six stations on the right side of the wall, where a single 60 m rope reaches each station but is tight at a couple of them, so parties carry a second rope or plan a short downclimb. The four-rappel line off M&M Ledge is a real descent, but it belongs to Thin Red Line rather than to this route; do not plan on it here.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.rappels: About 10 double-rope rappels (two 60 m ropes) down the X Couloir: four off pickets you place, one off a rock sling, five off existing slings on rock horns
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.rappel_count_note: One documented descent, a second descent of the couloir, made ten double-rope rappels: four off pickets the party placed, one off a sling around a rock, and five off slings already on rock horns lower in the gully. Carry two ropes, pickets you are willing to leave, and spare cord. In good snow, parties downclimb some of the face instead.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.descent_text: Most parties reverse the ascent line, downclimbing and rappelling the same southwest gully/couloir system (the X Couloir) back down into the southwest basin below the face. This is a real rappelling descent, not a walk-off: the most detailed documented descent (a repeat/'2nd descent' trip report) describes 10 double-rope rappels — 4 off pickets placed by the descending party, 1 off a sling around a rock, and 5 off pre-existing slings left around rock horns lower in the gully. Bring a rope long enough to rappel on doubled strands plus spare cord/webbing for building or backing up anchors, since fixed tat should never be trusted blindly. Anchors are a mix of natural (slung rock horns and blocks) and improvised (snow pickets), not bolted — expect to build some yourself. The exact rappel count is conditions-dependent: earlier-season parties with more continuous snow have gotten down with as few as 3 rappels off deadman/picket anchors and simul-downclimbing between them, while later-season, rockier conditions push the count up toward the 10-rappel figure above; budget for the higher number and extra anchor material. The gully funnels rockfall and is exposed to spindrift/small slides after storms, so descend early and move efficiently through the narrower constrictions. Once off the couloir, re-rope for the bergschrund and any crevassed ground on the way down to the treeline camp, then reverse the approach - down past East Rankin Lake and around Pt. 4481 on the old decommissioned road - back to FR-38. Do not descend north toward Heliotrope Ridge. With a camp in the Rankin Creek basin, going that way puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your camp.

wa_little_sister_south_couloir.rappels: Two rappels on the descent. One party made a double-60 m rappel from near the top of the line and a second rappel down from the col southeast of the summit; they noted a single 60 m rope would have been enough for the col rappel. Anchors are not fixed — bring cord and tat, and expect to build off rock horns or leave a picket/screw.
wa_little_sister_south_couloir.rappel_count_note: Two rappels, from one winter party's account: a double-rope rappel near the top of the line, and a single-rope rappel from the col southeast of the summit. Bring cord and tat; nothing is fixed.
wa_little_sister_south_couloir.descent_text: Reverse the line: one winter party made a double-rope rappel from near the top and a second rappel below the col southeast of the summit, where a single 60 m rope reaches. The couloir has also been skied.

wa_ellen_pea.rappels: 4 rappels on two 60 m ropes back down the route (about 15, 55, 50 and 40 m), mostly from bolted anchors; about an hour
wa_ellen_pea.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on two 60 m ropes: every rappel needs both ropes. Nearly every anchor is bolted below the top trees, and some rappels are diagonal, so steer to stay on line. About an hour from the top to the base. Instead of rappelling, you can traverse off to a 3rd-class ramp partway down.
wa_ellen_pea.descent_text: Descend via rappel using two ropes; expect some diagonal-rappel maneuvering to stay on anchors, or traverse off to a 3rd-class ramp partway down. Figure roughly an hour from the summit/top of the route back to the base.
